Show both paths . Step 1 — Download the data Download the files of the dataset you want to use and place them in a folder named after the dataset ( clisson/ or montagne/ ). These files are stored with Git LFS; the links below download the real content directly. Dataset Scene Typical run time (NoiseModelling) Folder Clisson Road-traffic noise map (line sources) ~30 min clisson/ La Montagne Single point source (a siren on a roof) ~5 min montagne/ Clisson — put these files in a folder named clisson/ File Size Link BUILDINGS.geojson 3.3 MB — DEM.geojson 53.1 MB — GROUNDS.geojson 1.1 MB — LW_ROADS.geojson 868 KB — RECEIVERS.geojson 254 KB — La Montagne — put these files in a folder named montagne/ File Size Link la_montagne_batiment.geojson 7.6 MB — DEM.geojson 219 MB large file — la_montagne_naturesol.geojson 187 KB — la_montagne_naturesol_G0.geojson 104 KB — la_montagne_naturesol_G_03.geojson 4.0 KB — la_montagne_naturesol_G_07.geojson 1.4 KB — la_montagne_naturesol_G_1.geojson 77.7 KB — LW_ROADS.geojson 359 B — RECEIVERS.geojson 6.0 KB — Large files: the DEM files are big (652 MB for Clisson, 219 MB for La Montagne) and can take a while to download — the other files are small. Clisson is a realistic road-traffic scene (many line sources): a full NoiseModelling run takes several minutes. La Montagne is a single point source (a siren on a roof) with only 10 receivers: it runs in under a minute, which makes it ideal for a first comparison. Step 2 — Run your own software Run your model on the dataset. The comparison works at the receiver level, so your software must produce one sound level per receiver . Export a GeoJSON FeatureCollection with one point per receiver, using exactly these two properties: IDRECEIVER — the receiver identifier. It is the PK value already present in the dataset's RECEIVERS.geojson (Clisson: 0…29410, La Montagne: 1…10). LAEQ — the computed A-weighted sound level in dB at that receiver. Expected output format (one feature per receiver) copy { "type": "Feature", "properties": { "IDRECEIVER": 10, "LAEQ": 84.2 }, "geometry": { "type": "Point", "coordinates": [345560.7, <sha>.6] } } For Clisson you can optionally add "PERIOD": "D" and the octave-band levels ( HZ63 … HZ8000 ) like the reference output; only IDRECEIVER and LAEQ are required for the comparison. The script writes output/RECEIVERS_LEVEL.geojson . Step 4 — Compare the two files Join your output with the NoiseModelling reference on IDRECEIVER and compare the LAEQ values. Two rules matter for a fair comparison: Silence threshold. In the benchmark, levels at or below −89 dB are treated as silence and excluded from the statistics. Apply the same rule. La Montagne calibration. The published La Montagne comparison is calibrated per version: an offset is applied so that the computed level equals the measured level at the receiver closest to the source. The raw output is not calibrated — calibration is only used on the results page. Share your results with the community Comparing independent implementations is how the community finds bugs and improves the models. Step 2 — Run your own software Run your model on the dataset. The comparison works at the receiver level, so your software must produce one sound level per receiver . Export a GeoJSON FeatureCollection with one point per receiver, using exactly these two properties: IDRECEIVER — the receiver identifier. It is the PK value already present in the dataset's RECEIVERS.geojson (Clisson: 0…29410, La Montagne: 1…10). LAEQ — the computed A-weighted sound level in dB at that receiver. Expected output format (one feature per receiver) copy { "type": "Feature", "properties": { "IDRECEIVER": 10, "LAEQ": 84.2 }, "geometry": { "type": "Point", "coordinates": [345560.7, <sha>.6] } } For Clisson you can optionally add "PERIOD": "D" and the octave-band levels ( HZ63 … HZ8000 ) like the reference output; only IDRECEIVER and LAEQ are required for the comparison. Two rules matter for a fair comparison: Silence threshold. In the benchmark, levels at or below −89 dB are treated as silence and excluded from the statistics. Apply the same rule. La Montagne calibration. The published La Montagne comparison is calibrated per version: an offset is applied so that the computed level equals the measured level at the receiver closest to the source. The raw output is not calibrated — calibration is only used on the results page.
